<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 4 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Tangent Spaces</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">4.3</span> Tensor Space <span class="math inline">\(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\)</span></h1></header>
<p>The concept of tensors generalizes that of vectors and covectors, providing a unified framework to describe multilinear geometric objects. While the definition of tensors is often introduced globally as tensor fields, it is conceptually clearer to begin with their local version at a point <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{M}\)</span>, constructed purely from the tangent and cotangent spaces <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>Tensors are often introduced as mysterious objects typically accompanied by the meaningless tautology “a tensor is an object that transforms like a tensor.” This unfortunate way of presenting tensors<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-9" id="fnref-9" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 9">9</a></sup> makes them appear more intimidating than they truly are. In reality, tensors are paper tigers.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Given a manifold <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A} \right)_d\)</span>, the <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange"><span class="math inline">\((r,s)\)</span>-tensor space</span> at <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> is the set of all multilinear maps of the form<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 10">10</a></sup> (Check Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../vector-spaces/vectors-duals-tensors.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Vectors_Duals_Tensors">2.2</a> for the definition of multilinearity):  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            T \colon
            \underbrace{T_p^*\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times T_p^*\mathcal{M}}_{r \text{-times}}
            \times
            \underbrace{T_p\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times T_p\mathcal{M}}_{s \text{-times}}
            &amp;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \dots \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \\
            \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(s)} \right)
            &amp;\longmapsto
            {T} \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(s)} \right),
        \end{align*}</span></p>
<p>Some particularly important cases of tensors are:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-2">
<li><p><span class="math inline">\((1, 0)\)</span>-tensors: elements of <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> (vectors).</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\((0, 1)\)</span>-tensors: elements of <span class="math inline">\(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> (covectors).</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\((0, 0)\)</span>-tensors: real numbers, i.e., elements of <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\((1, 1)\)</span>-tensors: linear maps (matrices) from <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> to itself.</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\((0, 2)\)</span>-tensors: bilinear forms, such as the metric (more on this in Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../metric/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Metric">7</a>).</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Alternatively, using tensor products, the space <span class="math inline">\(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\)</span> can be defined algebraically as the vector space (see §<a class="dg-xref" href="../vector-spaces/vectors-duals-tensors.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Vectors_Duals_Tensors">2.2</a>):  <span class="math display">\[
            T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} := \underbrace{T_p\mathcal{M} \otimes \dots \otimes T_p\mathcal{M}}_{r \text{-times}}
            \otimes
            \underbrace{T_p^*\mathcal{M} \otimes \dots \otimes T_p^*\mathcal{M}}_{s \text{-times}}.
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\(\left\{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \right\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left\{ (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\}\)</span> denote the bases of <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> associated with a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> around <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>, and let <span class="math inline">\(\left\{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p \right\}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left\{ (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p \right\}\)</span> denote the corresponding bases associated with a different chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\)</span>.</p>
<p>The components of a tensor <span class="math inline">\(T \in T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\)</span> w.r.t. the chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> are obtained by feeding it the basis elements of that chart,  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s}
            \coloneqq
            T\left( (d\mathscr{X}^{i_1})_p, \dots, (d\mathscr{X}^{i_r})_p,
            \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_1}} \right)_p, \dots, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_s}} \right)_p \right) \in \mathbb{R},
        \]</span>  in terms of which the tensor is expanded as  <span class="math display">\[
            T = \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}}
            \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s}
            \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}} \right)_p \otimes \dots \otimes \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_r}} \right)_p
            \otimes (d\mathscr{X}^{j_1})_p \otimes \dots \otimes (d\mathscr{X}^{j_s})_p.
        \]</span>  Denoting by <span class="math inline">\(\left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s}\)</span> the components w.r.t. the chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\)</span>, the transformation law for the components reads:  <span class="math display">\[
            \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s}
            =
            \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}}
            \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{k_1}} \right)_p \cdots
            \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_r}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{k_r}} \right)_p
            \cdot
            \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{l_1}}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_1}} \right)_p \cdots
            \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{l_s}}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_s}} \right)_p
            \cdot
            \left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s}.
        \]</span>  As we saw in Subsections <a class="dg-xref" href="tangent-space.html#subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM">4.1.1</a> and <a class="dg-xref" href="cotangent-space.html#subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TstarpM" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TstarpM">4.2.1</a>, each upper index (one per covector slot) transforms <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">contravariantly</span>, like the components of a vector, with a factor <span class="math inline">\(\left( \partial \mathscr{X}^{i} / \partial \mathscr{Y}^{k} \right)_p\)</span>, and each lower index (one per vector slot) transforms <span class="dg-term dg-term-orange">covariantly</span>, like the components of a covector, with a factor <span class="math inline">\(\left( \partial \mathscr{Y}^{l} / \partial \mathscr{X}^{j} \right)_p\)</span>.</p>
<p>By construction, the dimension of <span class="math inline">\(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\)</span> is <span class="math inline">\(\dim T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} = d^{r+s}\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-9" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-9" aria-label="Back to the text">9</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Common in many physics texts, perhaps stemming from the authors’ own apprehension toward differential geometry— a subject which, as the reader may have hopefully realized by this point, is in fact both harmless and remarkably beautiful.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-10" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-10" aria-label="Back to the text">10</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>The indices enclosed in parentheses, such as <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_{(j)}\)</span>, refer strictly to the position of the argument within the tensor map <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span>. They are not to be confused with coordinate indices or component labels. This is a purely positional convention used for clarity when expressing properties like multilinearity.</p></div></div></section>
